intro.text:
Have you ever wondered why a small alley off Hàng Bông Street is called Tạm Thương?

According to historical sources, the name comes from a temporary storehouse for tax rice in the early nineteenth century. The old granary is long gone, but the name has been kept through many generations.

Deeper inside the alley, you can find Yên Thái Communal House, which honors Imperial Consort Ỷ Lan, a prominent figure of the Lý dynasty.

Today, in place of the granary, there are stalls frying nem chua, the sound of conversation, and the snacking rhythm of Hanoi life.

In Tạm Thương, the name of an alley alone can open the story of many layers of urban life.

alleyStory.title: Tạm Thương Alley
paragraphs: The name Tạm Thương comes from the storage of provisions during the Nguyễn dynasty. According to Giang Quân's Dictionary of Hanoi Streets, as cited by VietnamPlus (2024a), an area of Yên Thái hamlet housed a temporary storehouse for tax rice in the early nineteenth century before it was moved to the main storehouse. It was called “Tạm Thương,” and the name later became the alley's name.

The alley bends several times, with Yên Thái Communal House as a notable landmark. The house honors Imperial Consort Ỷ Lan and preserves artifacts such as a stone stele, a bronze bell, royal edicts, and traditional worship objects (Hoàn Kiếm Tourism Portal, n.d.).
VietnamPlus (2024a) records memories of a snake-wine shop that once operated in the alley and how the area changed over time. Today, Tạm Thương is known for fried nem chua and snack shops.
Distinctive character: The alley's name preserves its former granary function, a communal-house space amid the city, and its transformation into a food alley.

nodes.name: Yên Thái Communal House
nodes.summary: A place of worship for Imperial Consort Ỷ Lan, linked to the history of Yên Thái hamlet and local community beliefs.
nodes.story: At number eight Tạm Thương Alley is Yên Thái Communal House, also called Quán Linh Từ, where reports say Imperial Consort Ỷ Lan is worshipped. A newspaper records that the site was listed as a national heritage monument in nineteen ninety-five. Available sources do not establish when the house was first built; surviving royal decrees span the eighteenth to twentieth centuries. From this account of local belief, we turn to the Vọng Tiên legend on Hàng Bông Street.

nodes.name: Vọng Tiên Temple
nodes.summary: A Mother Goddess shrine linked to the legend of King Lê Thánh Tông meeting a celestial maiden.
nodes.story: The main story for this leg is the Vọng Tiên Temple on Hàng Bông Street, at number one hundred twenty B. According to legend, King Lê Thánh Tông met a young woman beside Ngọc Hồ; after she vanished, he had Vọng Tiên Pavilion built in her memory. This is a folk story, not a verified historical event. The sources I checked identify the temple as a place of Mother Goddess worship, but do not place it inside Tạm Thương Alley.
